A barfly is a person who spends an excessive amount of time at bars, drinking. Not someone who occasionally goes out for a drink with friends — but someone who seems to live at the bar. Day after day, night after night, you can reliably find this person perched on a barstool, glass in hand. The bar has essentially become their second home, or sometimes their first.

This is not a neutral word. Calling someone a barfly is mildly critical — even a little pitying. It paints a picture of someone whose life seems to revolve around alcohol and bar culture, with not much else going on. It suggests a certain aimlessness. You wouldn't call a successful, busy professional who enjoys a weekend drink a barfly. The word is reserved for someone who is a fixture at the bar — someone the bartender knows by name, whose usual drink is already being poured before they even sit down.

It's informal and colloquial. You'd say it in conversation or find it in casual writing — not in a formal or professional context.
The Visual Picture Behind the Word

Think about how a common fly behaves. It doesn't just visit a place once — it hovers, lands, returns, lingers. It's annoyingly persistent. Now apply that image to a person and a bar. A barfly is someone who "hangs around" bars the way a fly hangs around food — persistently, habitually, and with a kind of magnetic pull toward the place. The image makes the word vivid and slightly unflattering at the same time.

• It does not mean the same as alcoholic, which is a clinical word referring to a medical condition of addiction. A barfly is defined by where they spend their time, not by a diagnosis. (Though the implication of heavy drinking is certainly there.)
  • It does not mean someone who simply enjoys bars socially. Casual, occasional bar-goers are not barflies.
  • It is not a compliment, but it's also not a harsh insult. It's more of a wry, slightly sarcastic observation.
How It Differs From Similar Words

ConceptWhat Makes It Different From "Barfly"

Words like drunk or drunkard focus on the state of being intoxicated. A barfly, by contrast, is defined by the habit and location — the constant presence at the bar — rather than purely the drinking itself. The word lush focuses on someone who drinks heavily in general. The word regular (as in, a regular at a restaurant) is a neutral term for someone who frequently visits a place — a barfly is specifically a bar regular, with a negative undertone that "regular" doesn't carry.

• "Don't bother calling him in the evenings — he's become a complete barfly since he retired."
  • "The old dive bar was packed with barflies who had nowhere better to be."
  • "She used to be so driven, but now she's just a barfly who tells the same stories every night."

A barfly is someone who habitually and excessively haunts bars, drinking. The word is informal, mildly judgmental, and carries the image of a person who is a persistent, almost permanent presence at the bar — like a fly that just won't leave. It says less about clinical addiction and more about a lifestyle of aimless, heavy bar-dwelling.
